concepts.title: Nucleotide Anatomy and the Polynucleotide Chain
concepts.definition: A nucleotide assembles from three parts -- a nitrogenous base, a five-carbon sugar and a phosphate group; base plus sugar forms a nucleoside through an N-glycosidic bond, adding phosphate builds the nucleotide, and 3'-5' phosphodiester bonds string nucleotides into a chain whose backbone is sugar-phosphate with the bases jutting outward.
concepts.key_idea: Sugar type and base identity are the only switches separating dna building blocks from rna ones -- deoxyribose versus ribose, thymine versus uracil.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebo105.txt lines 60-98 (polynucleotide chain chemistry, DNA length examples)
question_patterns: name the three components of a nucleotide
how does a nucleoside differ from a nucleotide
which bond joins two nucleotides together in a dna strand
which purines and pyrimidines occur in dna and rna
why does every rna residue carry a hydroxyl group that dna lacks
explain what the 5' and 3' ends of a polynucleotide chain mean

solution_steps.explain: A nitrogenous base attaches at the 1' carbon of the pentose sugar (N-glycosidic bond) to give a nucleoside; phosphorylation at the 5' carbon upgrades it to a nucleotide.
The phosphate of one nucleotide links the 3' hydroxyl of the next, so every chain has a free 5' phosphate end and a free 3' hydroxyl end.
Adenine and guanine are purines; cytosine, thymine and uracil are pyrimidines -- thymine is dna-only, uracil replaces it in rna.
Rna's ribose carries an extra hydroxyl at the 2' position; its length is measured in nucleotides or base pairs, a signature of each organism.

concepts.title: Watson-Crick Double Helix and Base Pairing
concepts.definition: Two antiparallel sugar-phosphate strands coil right-handedly around a common axis; inside, adenine faces thymine over two hydrogen bonds and guanine faces cytosine over three, so a purine always opposes a pyrimidine, the strands hold an even gap, and roughly ten base pairs fill each 3.4 nm turn of the helix.
concepts.key_idea: Complementarity is the master stroke -- either strand predicts its partner, exactly what a heritable molecule needs for faithful copying.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebo105.txt lines 99-167 (1953 model, Chargaff observation, five salient features, central dogma)
question_patterns: list the salient features of the dna double helix proposed by watson and crick
how many hydrogen bonds join adenine to thymine and guanine to cytosine
why does a purine always sit opposite a pyrimidine in dna
what does antiparallel polarity mean for the two strands of dna
how many base pairs fit into one complete turn of the dna helix
whose x-ray diffraction images supported the 1953 dna model

solution_steps.explain: One chain runs 5'-to-3' while its partner runs 3'-to-5'; both backbones are outside and the bases point inward.

solution_steps.action: Pair the bases by bond count
solution_steps.explain: A-T pairs share two hydrogen bonds, G-C pairs share three; pairing big purine with small pyrimidine keeps the helix diameter uniform.
The right-handed coil advances 3.4 nm per turn with about 10 bp stacked per turn, roughly 0.34 nm between neighbours.
Stacked pairs plus hydrogen bonding stabilise the helix, and complementarity implies each strand templates the other -- the logic behind copying and the dna-to-rna-to-protein flow of information.

concepts.title: Chargaff's Rule and Base Percentages
concepts.definition: In any double-stranded dna the adenine tally matches thymine and guanine matches cytosine, so each complementary pair owns a fixed share of the molecule; measuring one base pins down the other three by simple arithmetic.
concepts.key_idea: Pair equality is the arithmetic fingerprint of a two-stranded helix -- and it breaks down for single-stranded molecules.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebo105.txt lines 106-110 (Chargaff ratios) and exercise 2, lines 1211-1213
question_patterns: calculate the adenine percentage when the cytosine content of dna is given
state chargaff's rule for double stranded dna
if a dna sample holds 20 percent cytosine what percent of it is adenine
why must the amounts of a and t be equal inside a double helix
work out all four base percentages from one measured value
does chargaff's rule apply to single stranded dna molecules

solution_steps.explain: Cytosine pairs only with guanine in equal amounts, so together they occupy twice the cytosine percentage, leaving the rest of the molecule for the a-t pair.
Adenine and thymine are also equal partners, so adenine takes half of that remainder.

concepts.title: Packaging the Helix: Nucleosomes and Chromatin
concepts.definition: A mammalian nucleus must cram a helix metres long into a compartment a million times smaller; negatively charged dna winds around discs made of eight positively charged histone proteins, producing nucleosomes -- about 200 bp apiece -- whose string coils up into chromatin fibres and ultimately metaphase chromosomes, with loose euchromatin staying readable and dense heterochromatin switched off.
concepts.key_idea: Opposite charges do the packing -- basic histones grip acidic dna -- and packing density decides whether a region's genes can be transcribed.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebo105.txt lines 168-217 (length calculation, nucleoid, histone octamer, beads-on-string, euchromatin vs heterochromatin)
question_patterns: how does a two-metre-long dna molecule fit inside a tiny nucleus
describe a nucleosome and name the proteins forming its core
what produces the beads-on-string look of chromatin under the microscope
differentiate euchromatin from heterochromatin in structure and activity
how many base pairs wrap around a single nucleosome
contrast dna organisation in prokaryotes with that in eukaryotes

solution_steps.explain: Multiplying base pairs by 0.34 nm each gives about 2.2 metres of helix per mammalian diploid cell against a nucleus around a micrometre across.
Without a nucleus, e. coli holds its dna in looped domains anchored by proteins in a nucleoid region.
Histones rich in lysine and arginine form an octamer; dna wraps around it to make a nucleosome, the repeating bead of chromatin.
Beads-on-string folds into fibres with non-histone proteins; light-staining, gene-active stretches are euchromatin while dark, inert stretches are heterochromatin.

concepts.title: The Search for Genetic Material: Griffith to Hershey-Chase
concepts.definition: Griffith watched harmless bacteria turn lethal after mingling with heat-killed virulent ones and credited an unknown transforming principle; Avery, MacLeod and McCarty pinned the principle to dna by digesting each candidate in turn, and Hershey and Chase closed the case with radiolabelled phages whose phosphorus-tagged dna -- never their sulfur-tagged protein -- slipped into the bacteria.
concepts.key_idea: Three experiments in a row narrowed the answer from something to protein-versus-dna to dna alone.
question_patterns: what did griffith observe in his experiments with streptococcus pneumoniae
explain the transforming principle that griffith demonstrated
how did avery macleod and mccarty identify the transforming substance
why did protease and rnase treatments fail to stop transformation while dnase succeeded
describe the hershey and chase blender experiment and its conclusion
why were radioactive phosphorus and radioactive sulfur the right labels for dna and protein

solution_steps.explain: Mice given live rough (R) cells survived, given smooth (S) cells died, given heat-killed S cells survived -- but a mix of the last two killed, with live S cells recovered.
Something passed from the dead S cells and permanently equipped R cells to make a polysaccharide coat -- Griffith's transforming principle, of unknown chemistry.
Protease and rnase left transformation intact; dnase abolished it, so dna -- not protein or rna -- carries the transforming information.
Phage dna labelled with phosphorus-32 entered the bacterial cells and progeny phages followed; sulfur-35-labelled protein coats stayed outside after blending -- dna is the hereditary molecule.

concepts.title: DNA versus RNA as Genetic Material and the RNA World
concepts.definition: A genetic molecule must copy itself, keep its structure, admit slow mutation and be expressible; dna outscores rna on stability because it drops the reactive 2' hydroxyl and swaps uracil for thymine, while rna's restlessness suits messenger, adapter and catalytic jobs -- clues that rna ran the earliest cells and dna was refined out of it later.
concepts.key_idea: Storage favours the stable molecule (dna), dynamic messaging and catalysis favour the reactive one (rna) -- and life very likely began in an rna-only world.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebo105.txt lines 301-375 (criteria for genetic material, stability argument, RNA world)
question_patterns: why is dna regarded as a better genetic material than rna
list the four properties a molecule needs to serve as genetic material
which chemical group makes rna chemically unstable
why do biologists think rna was the first genetic material
name the jobs rna performs besides acting as a genome in some viruses
how does thymine in place of uracil add stability to dna

solution_steps.explain: Base pairing lets dna and rna alike self-copy, mutate and be expressed; proteins fail at the copying step outright.
Rna's 2' hydroxyl makes it labile and easily degraded while dna is chemically calmer; heat-separated dna strands even re-anneal, which explains why Griffith's heat-killed cells still transformed.
Rna mutates faster (useful for rapid evolution), codes for protein directly, and doubles as catalyst; dna stores information more safely, so genomes that must persist choose dna.
Metabolism, translation and splicing grew up around rna, which served as both genome and enzyme before dna emerged as the stabilized archive.

concepts.title: Semiconservative Replication and the Meselson-Stahl Proof
concepts.definition: Every daughter helix keeps one original strand and receives one freshly built partner -- the semiconservative scheme that Watson and Crick read directly out of base pairing; Meselson and Stahl shifted heavy-nitrogen-grown bacteria to a light medium and watched the hybrid-then-mixed density pattern that only this scheme predicts.
concepts.key_idea: Heavy nitrogen density-labelling separated old strands from new without needing any radioactivity.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebo105.txt lines 376-440 (Watson-Crick proposal, Meselson-Stahl 1958, Taylor's Vicia faba experiment)
question_patterns: what does semiconservative replication imply for the two dna strands
describe the meselson and stahl experiment that proved dna replication is semiconservative
after three generations in a light medium what fraction of dna molecules still have hybrid density
why did the experiment use a cesium chloride density gradient instead of radioactivity
which property of the double helix suggested its own copying mechanism to watson and crick
how did taylor confirm semiconservative replication in faba bean chromosomes

solution_steps.explain: Each round of division halves the pool of molecules still carrying a heavy parental strand.
Everything else now holds two light strands, so subtract from one.

concepts.title: Replication Machinery: Enzymes, Fork and Origin
concepts.definition: dna-dependent dna polymerase lengthens chains only in the 5'-to-3' direction, so one template is read continuously while its partner is copied in short pieces that dna ligase later seals; unwinding happens locally at the replication fork, initiation occurs only at special origins, and the deoxynucleoside triphosphate substrates bankroll the reaction with their own high-energy phosphates.
concepts.key_idea: One-directional polymerisation forces the asymmetric fork -- a continuous leading side and a discontinuous, ligase-stitched lagging side.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebo105.txt lines 441-491 (polymerase, rate ~2000 bp/s, replication fork, ligase, origin, S-phase)
question_patterns: why can dna polymerase build a new strand only in the 5 to 3 direction
explain the difference between continuous and discontinuous synthesis at the replication fork
which enzyme stitches together the short fragments made on the lagging strand
what is an origin of replication and why must a cloning vector carry one
at what rate must polymerisation run for e coli to copy its genome within 18 minutes
what dual role do deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates play during replication

solution_steps.explain: dna polymerase uses a dna template to string deoxynucleotides together, fast and accurate -- e. coli manages roughly 2000 bp per second with few errors.
Whole-length strand separation costs too much energy, so the helix opens only in a small pocket that travels along -- the replication fork.
The 3'-to-5' template accepts continuous synthesis; the 5'-to-3' template forces short segments that dna ligase joins afterwards.
Polymerase cannot begin from nothing and initiation is restricted to defined origins -- the reason recombinant dna needs a vector supplying one; in eukaryotes the whole schedule is pinned to S phase.

concepts.title: Transcription Unit: Promoter, Gene, Terminator
concepts.definition: A transcription unit stretches from a promoter, through the structural gene, to a terminator; only one strand is copied -- the 3'-to-5' template -- while its partner, matching the rna letter-for-letter except for thymine, oddly gets the name coding strand, and which strand plays which role is decided purely by where the promoter sits.
concepts.key_idea: Copying both strands would make complementary rnas that anneal into a dead double strand -- so one strand, one direction, sharply marked boundaries.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebo105.txt lines 492-552 (definition of transcription, why one strand, unit boundaries, strand conventions)
question_patterns: name the three regions that define a transcription unit in dna
distinguish the template strand from the coding strand
why is only one strand of dna copied during transcription
where do the promoter and terminator sit relative to the structural gene
what decides which of the two dna strands acts as the template
write down the rna sequence transcribed from a given template strand

solution_steps.explain: The promoter (upstream, 5' side of the coding strand) hosts polymerase binding; the terminator (downstream, 3' side) ends the run; between them lies the structural gene.
Polymerase works 5'-to-3', so the 3'-to-5' strand is read as the template; the other strand echoes the rna sequence (T for U) and is called coding.
Two templates would yield two different rna products and, worse, mutually complementary rnas that pair up and never reach the ribosome.
Copying follows the pairing rule except that adenosine in dna pairs with uracil in rna.

concepts.title: RNA Polymerases, Split Genes and mRNA Processing
concepts.definition: Bacteria run all rna synthesis through a single polymerase that starts with a sigma factor and stops with rho, whereas eukaryotes divide the labour among three polymerases and must edit their interrupted genes -- splicing introns out of exons, capping the 5' end and tailing the 3' end -- before the finished mrna may leave the nucleus.
concepts.key_idea: Split genes and rna editing are living traces of the rna world; bacteria skip the editing because transcription and translation share one compartment.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebo105.txt lines 553-638 (cistron, exons/introns, three RNA types, bacterial vs eukaryotic transcription, splicing/capping/tailing)
question_patterns: which eukaryotic rna polymerase transcribes rrna trna and the mrna precursor
what are exons and introns in a split gene
explain splicing capping and tailing of the primary transcript
how do sigma and rho factors steer bacterial transcription
why can bacteria couple transcription with translation but eukaryotes cannot
define a cistron and contrast monocistronic with polycistronic transcripts

solution_steps.explain: A cistron -- a dna segment coding for one polypeptide -- lets us label structural genes monocistronic (mostly eukaryotic) or polycistronic (mostly bacterial); even trna and rrna genes count as genes.
One rna polymerase initiates at the promoter with sigma, elongates, and releases at the terminator with rho; mrna needs no editing and is translated even while still being made.
Polymerase I builds rrnas, polymerase III builds trna and 5s rrna, and polymerase II transcribes hnRNA, the precursor of mrna.
Splicing removes introns and joins exons in order; a methyl guanosine triphosphate cap goes on the 5' end and 200-300 adenylates form the 3' tail before the mature mrna exits the nucleus.

concepts.title: The Genetic Code: Triplet, Degenerate, Universal
concepts.definition: Three nucleotide letters per codon is the shortest scheme letting four bases spell all twenty amino acids -- four cubed yields 64 codons, sixty-one with meanings and three stop signals; the message reads continuously with no punctuation, holds nearly unchanged from bacteria to humans, doubles aug as methionine codon and start signal, and keeps multiple synonyms for most amino acids.
concepts.key_idea: Degeneracy cushions point mutations -- with several synonyms per amino acid, a single-base error often swaps in a harmless synonym.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebo105.txt lines 639-701 (Gamow's triplet logic, Khorana/Nirenberg/Ochoa, six salient features)
question_patterns: why must the genetic code use a triplet of bases
how many codons specify amino acids and how many act as stop signals
state the salient features of the genetic code
what makes aug a special codon
explain the degeneracy of the genetic code with an example
work out how many codons four bases can generate in groups of three

solution_steps.explain: Four different bases serve as the letters of the code.
Three positions with four choices each give four-cubed distinct codons.

concepts.title: Frameshift Mutations and the Reading Frame
concepts.definition: Inserting or deleting one or two bases knocks every downstream codon out of register because the three-letter reading frame slips, while adding or removing three bases -- or any multiple of three -- merely adds or drops whole amino acids and leaves the remainder of the message intact.
concepts.key_idea: The three-letter-word sentence analogy shows why only multiples of three keep a gene's message readable.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebo105.txt lines 702-739 (point mutation recap, RAM HAS RED CAP frameshift analogy)
question_patterns: what is a frameshift mutation and when does it arise
why does inserting three bases do less harm than inserting one
explain the ram has red cap analogy used for the genetic code
how does a single base insertion corrupt every codon after it
which mutation class removes whole amino acids without disturbing the frame
connect sickle cell anaemia to a point mutation in the beta globin gene

solution_steps.explain: Ribosomes read mrna in fixed three-base steps with no gaps, so codon boundaries depend on where the first base sits.
An insertion or deletion of one or two bases re-partitions the whole downstream sequence into wrong triplets -- a frameshift -- changing every subsequent amino acid.
Adding or losing a full codon's worth of bases inserts or deletes exactly one amino acid but restores the frame for everything after.
A single-base replacement, as in the beta globin gene of sickle-cell anaemia, changes at most one amino acid rather than derailing the message.

concepts.title: Translation: tRNA, Ribosome and Polypeptide Synthesis
concepts.definition: Amino acids have no way of reading codons themselves, so trna adapters each pick up their own amino acid and match their anticodon loop to the mrna message; the ribosome then welds the cargo together -- its 23s rrna even catalyses the peptide bond -- marching from the aug start codon until a release factor meets a stop codon and frees the finished polypeptide.
concepts.key_idea: Every peptide bond costs energy, paid up front when atp charges each trna with its amino acid.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebo105.txt lines 740-815 (tRNA adapter, charging, ribosome structure, UTRs, translation phases)
question_patterns: why is trna described as the adapter molecule
describe the anticodon loop and amino acid acceptor end of trna
what happens during the charging of trna
list the phases of translation from initiation through elongation to termination
which ribosomal component acts as the enzyme for peptide bond formation
what are untranslated regions of mrna and what good are they

solution_steps.explain: Each amino acid is activated by atp and attached to its own trna (aminoacylation); an initiator trna exists for aug, and stop codons have none.
The ribosome splits into subunits; the small one finds the mrna and the aug start codon, while the large one offers two sites that hold neighbouring charged trnas close enough to bond.
Anticodon-codon pairing places each amino acid; the 23s rrna ribozyme forms the peptide bond and the ribosome steps along the message.
At a stop codon a release factor takes the slot, the completed polypeptide detaches, and untranslated regions flanking the coding stretch help regulate the whole process.

concepts.title: Lac Operon: Negative Regulation by an Inducer
concepts.definition: The lac operon of Jacob and Monod bundles a repressor gene (i) with three lactose-processing genes (z, y, a) under one promoter; the constitutively made repressor parks on the operator and blocks transcription until lactose, acting as inducer, disarms it -- so beta-galactosidase, permease and transacetylase appear only when the sugar is actually available.
concepts.key_idea: A substrate switching on the enzymes that digest it is the classic case of negative control in bacteria.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebo105.txt lines 816-898 (levels of regulation, operon concept, i/z/y/a genes, inducer mechanism)
question_patterns: how does lactose switch the lac operon on
name the structural genes of the lac operon and what each product does
what part does the operator region play in operon function
why is lac operon control described as negative regulation
what happens to the operon once the lactose supply runs out
why must a trickle of lac operon expression continue even without lactose

solution_steps.explain: Gene i makes the repressor; z gives beta-galactosidase (lactose into glucose plus galactose), y gives permease (lets beta-galactosides in), a gives transacetylase -- all sharing one promoter and operator.
The repressor is always being made and binds the operator, physically barring rna polymerase from transcribing the cluster.
Lactose entering through basal permease meets the repressor and inactivates it; the promoter clears and transcription proceeds -- a substrate regulating its own enzyme synthesis.
A very low constitutive expression must persist, otherwise permease would vanish and lactose could never re-enter to induce the operon; glucose and galactose cannot induce it.

concepts.title: Human Genome Project: Goals, Methods and Findings
concepts.definition: Launched in 1990 and wrapped up in 2003, the human genome project read all three billion base pairs using expressed sequence tags plus blind whole-genome sequencing cloned into bacterial or yeast artificial chromosomes, automated sanger-style reads and computer assembly; it settled on roughly twenty thousand to twenty-five thousand genes and revealed that repeats dominate the genome.
concepts.key_idea: Under two percent of the genome codes for protein, chromosome 1 carries the most genes and the y the fewest, and snp mapping transformed the hunt for disease loci.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebo105.txt lines 903-1055 (mega project scale, goals, EST vs annotation, salient features, applications)
question_patterns: what were the major goals of the human genome project
contrast the expressed sequence tag strategy with sequence annotation
which vectors and host cells were used to clone genome fragments
list the salient findings about the human genome that the project produced
why is the human genome project labelled a mega project
estimate how many printed books would hold the entire human genome sequence

solution_steps.explain: Three billion base pairs at early prices meant billions of dollars and thousands of printed volumes -- hence bioinformatics grew alongside it.
One route catalogued expressed sequence tags; the other sequenced everything blindly and assigned functions afterwards (annotation).
Dna was fragmented, cloned in bacteria or yeast via BAC and YAC vectors, read on sanger-method automated sequencers, then aligned by overlapping regions with specialist software.

About 3164.7 million bp, average gene 3000 bases (dystrophin the giant at 2.4 million), 99.9 percent of bases identical between people, over half the genome repetitive, chromosome 1 richest in genes (2968), y poorest (231), and about 1.4 million snp positions catalogued.

concepts.title: DNA Fingerprinting: Satellite DNA, VNTR and Uses
concepts.definition: Tandemly repeated satellite sequences scattered through the genome code for no protein yet differ enormously in repeat count from person to person; Alec Jeffreys exploited these variable mini-satellites as probes -- isolate, digest, separate, blot, hybridise, autoradiograph -- yielding a band pattern unique to everyone except identical twins, the foundation of forensic and paternity testing.
concepts.key_idea: Repetitive non-coding dna accumulates variation freely because changes there rarely harm reproduction, which is what makes each person's band pattern personal.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebo105.txt lines 1056-1151 (satellite vs bulk DNA, polymorphism definition, VNTR technique steps, applications)
question_patterns: what is dna fingerprinting and which sequences does it depend on
how does satellite dna separate from bulk genomic dna during centrifugation
list the steps of the vntr southern blot fingerprinting method
why is dna fingerprinting trusted in forensic and paternity disputes
what does polymorphism in dna sequence mean and how does it arise
how does pcr extend dna fingerprinting to samples of a single cell

solution_steps.explain: Density gradient spinning splits bulk dna (major peak) from satellite dna (small peaks); tandem repeats there show extreme polymorphism -- a variant counts as polymorphic when it exceeds one percent frequency in the population.
Isolate dna, cut with restriction enzymes, electrophorese, blot onto a membrane, hybridise with a labelled vntr probe, and read the autoradiogram's band pattern.
Repeat copy number varies chromosome by chromosome and person by person, so bands match only for identical twins -- every tissue of one individual gives the same fingerprint.
Because polymorphisms are inherited, fingerprints settle paternity and track population diversity; amplifying dna by pcr lets one cell suffice.

worked_examples.question_pattern: Heavy-nitrogen bacteria are shifted to a light medium and allowed to divide for {generations} generations. What fraction of the dna molecules is then fully light, and what fraction still shows hybrid density?

solution_template.explain: Only molecules descending with a heavy parental strand keep hybrid density, and their share halves every generation.
Subtracting the hybrid share from the whole leaves the fully light molecules.

worked_examples.source_ref: lebo105.txt lines 914-927 (mega project scale and the books analogy)
worked_examples.question_pattern: Printing the human genome needs {base_pairs} letters of sequence, {letters_per_page} letters to a page and {pages_per_book} pages per book. How many books would one person's sequence fill?

solution_template.explain: Each book carries letters per page times pages per book.
Dividing the sequence length by a book's capacity gives the library size.
